title: Lusus Troiae. Naves incensae
titleEn: The Game of Troy and the Burning of the Ships — Aeneid V.580–679
source: P. Vergilius Maro, Aeneid, ed. J. B. Greenough, The Bucolics, Aeneid, and Georgics of Virgil (Boston: Ginn & Company, 1881), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0690.phi003.perseus-lat2, sha256 e639e6a0e27427ef. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Greenough's spelling kept (volnus, divom, Karthago, -is accusatives); his quotation marks printed as “ ”. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: The boys' ride for Anchises goes on: the three troops part, wheel, charge and fall back, and weave their courses in and out like the paths of the Labyrinth in Crete or dolphins playing in the sea. Virgil tells how Ascanius brought this display, the 'Troy game', to Alba Longa when he walled it, and how Alba handed it down to Rome, where boys still ride it under the name of Troy. Then fortune turns. While the men keep the games at the tomb, Juno, still nursing her old grievance, sends Iris down her rainbow to the fleet. On a lonely stretch of shore the Trojan women are weeping for Anchises and looking out at the sea, sick of it, longing for a city. Iris takes the shape of old Beroë, a woman of good family, and urges them: seven summers of wandering are enough, here are Eryx's lands and a friendly host, and Cassandra came to her in a dream with burning torches and told them their Troy is here; so let them burn the ships. She hurls the first torch. Old Pyrgo, nurse to Priam's sons, warns that this is no Beroë, whom she left sick at home, but a goddess, as her eyes, breath and step betray. The women waver until Iris rises away on her wings and cuts a great bow beneath the clouds; then, frenzied by the portent, they snatch fire from hearths and altars, and the flames run through the benches, oars and painted sterns. Eumelus brings the news to the games; Ascanius, straight from leading his horsemen, gallops to the camp, flings off his helmet and cries that they are burning their own hopes. Aeneas and the Trojans follow, and the women scatter in shame to the woods and caves, their minds come back to them and Juno shaken out of their hearts.
part: The Game of Troy and the Burning of the Ships (V.580–679)

sentences.t:
Olli discurrere pares, atque agmina terni
diductis solvere choris, rursusque vocati
convertere vias infestaque tela tulere.
sentences.l:
They ran apart in matching ranks, and their columns, in threes,
with bands drawn asunder they loosened, and again, called back,
they turned round their ways and their hostile weapons bore.
sentences.i: They galloped apart in matching ranks, and the three troops broke their columns, parting into separate bands; then, called back, they wheeled about and bore down with levelled spears.
sentences.n: A new paragraph: the boys' ride, begun at the end of the last part, now goes through its movements. 'Olli' is an old form of 'illi', 'they', one of Virgil's deliberate archaisms. 'Discurrere', 'solvere', 'convertere' and 'tulere' are all perfects in '-ere' for '-erunt' (you'll see this constantly). 'Pares' is 'equal', 'matched', the riders keeping even ranks. 'Terni' is a distributive numeral, 'three each', 'in threes', agreeing with the riders, not with 'agmina', used here for the three troops; 'agmina… solvere' is 'they broke up their columns', and 'diductis… choris' is an ablative absolute, 'their bands drawn apart' ('chorus', properly a dancing band, suits a display ride). 'Vocati' is the perfect participle passive of 'voco', 'called back' (by the signal). 'Convertere vias' is 'they turned their courses round', and 'infesta tela tulere' is 'they carried their weapons levelled', as for a charge.

sentences.i: Then they enter on new charges and new retreats, facing one another across the field, and interlace circle with circle, and in their armour call up the semblance of a battle;
sentences.n: 'Inde' is 'next', 'then'. 'Alios… cursus aliosque recursus' is 'other runs and other runs back', the 'cursus… recursus' pair making the to-and-fro audible. 'Adversi' is 'facing (each other)', and 'spatiis' an ablative of place, 'on their tracks', 'across the spaces' of the field. 'Alternos… orbibus orbes impediunt' is 'they entangle alternating circles with circles', 'alternos' agreeing with the accusative 'orbes', and 'orbibus' a dative or ablative with 'impediunt'. 'Cient' is the present of 'cieo', 'stir up', 'set in motion'. 'Pugnae… simulacra' is 'images of a fight', a mock battle; 'sub armis' is 'in arms', 'under arms'.

sentences.t:
et nunc terga fuga nudant, nunc spicula vertunt
infensi, facta pariter nunc pace feruntur.
sentences.l:
and now their backs in flight they bare, now their spears they turn,
hostile, now, peace made, side by side they are carried.
sentences.i: and now they lay bare their backs in flight, now turn their spear-points against each other in attack, now, with peace made, ride on side by side.
sentences.n: 'Nunc… nunc… nunc' is anaphora, three phases of the ride. 'Terga fuga nudant' is 'they bare their backs in flight', 'fuga' an ablative of manner: to turn away is to expose one's back. 'Spicula vertunt' is 'they turn their spear-points' (back on the pursuer). 'Infensi' is 'hostile', 'with hostile intent', predicative. 'Facta… pace' is an ablative absolute, 'peace having been made'. 'Pariter' is 'side by side', 'together', and 'feruntur' is a passive with middle sense, 'they ride', 'they are borne along' (on horseback).

sentences.t:
Ut quondam Creta fertur Labyrinthus in alta
parietibus textum caecis iter, ancipitemque
mille viis habuisse dolum, qua signa sequendi
falleret indeprensus et inremeabilis error;
sentences.l:
As once in Crete, it is said, the Labyrinth in high
with blind walls a woven path, and a two-way
with a thousand roads to have had trickery, where the signs of following
would baffle the undiscoverable and unretraceable wandering;
sentences.i: As once, so the story goes, the Labyrinth in lofty Crete held a path woven between blind walls, and a baffling trick of a thousand ways, where the maze, past finding out and past retracing, would defeat every sign that might guide the steps;
sentences.n: A simile. The Labyrinth was the maze Daedalus built in Crete for King Minos to house the Minotaur, which Theseus found his way out of by a thread. 'Ut quondam… fertur… habuisse' is 'as once… is said to have had', a personal passive of report ('fertur', 'is said') with the perfect infinitive. 'Creta… in alta' is 'in lofty Crete'. 'Parietibus textum caecis iter' is 'a path woven with blind walls', 'parietibus' an ablative of means (the word is 'paries', the wall of a building; in this line its first 'i' is taken as a consonant, so that it scans in four syllables, par-ie-ti-bus), 'caecis' 'blind', agreeing with 'parietibus', walls that give no view through. 'Ancipitem… dolum' is 'a two-sided trick', 'ancipitem' 'double', 'doubtful', and 'mille viis' an ablative of quality or means, 'with a thousand ways'. 'Qua' is 'where', 'by which', and 'falleret' a subjunctive in a relative clause of purpose or characteristic: 'such that the wandering would cheat the signs'. 'Signa sequendi' is 'the marks for following', 'sequendi' a gerund in the genitive. The subject is 'error', 'the wandering', the maze itself, with 'indeprensus' 'not to be detected' and 'inremeabilis' 'not to be retraced' (Greenough's spelling for 'irremeabilis'). The Latin Library prints 'frangeret', 'would break', for 'falleret', 'would baffle', a difference of sense, though the picture is the same.

sentences.t:
haud alio Teucrum nati vestigia cursu
impediunt texuntque fugas et proelia ludo,
delphinum similes, qui per maria umida nando
[Carpathium Libycumque secant, luduntque per undas.]
sentences.l:
not by other course of the Teucrians the sons their tracks
entangle, and weave flights and battles in play,
like dolphins, who through the seas, wet, by swimming
[the Carpathian and the Libyan cleave, and play through the waves.]
sentences.i: even so the sons of the Trojans tangle their tracks and weave flights and battles in sport, like dolphins swimming through the watery seas, [who cleave the Carpathian and the Libyan waters and play among the waves.]
sentences.n: 'Haud alio… cursu' is 'with no other course', 'not otherwise', taking up the 'ut' of the simile. 'Teucrum' is the old genitive plural in '-um' for '-orum' (you'll see this constantly), 'of the Teucrians', the Trojans, with 'nati', 'sons', as subject. 'Vestigia… impediunt' is 'they entangle their tracks', taking up 'impediunt' of 585, and 'texunt' 'weave' takes up 'textum' of 589: the boys' ride is the maze. 'Ludo' is an ablative of manner, 'in play'. 'Delphinum similes' is 'like dolphins', 'similis' with the genitive. 'Nando' is a gerund in the ablative, 'by swimming'. Greenough prints 595 in square brackets as spurious (a line he judges not Virgil's), and it is kept in brackets; the Latin Library prints the line too, but without 'luduntque per undas'. If the whole line is dropped, the relative 'qui… nando' is left without a verb. 'Carpathium Libycumque' are adjectives with 'mare' understood from 'maria': the Carpathian sea (between Crete and Rhodes) and the Libyan sea, south of Crete.

sentences.t:
Hunc morem cursus atque haec certamina primus
Ascanius, Longam muris cum cingeret Albam,
rettulit, et priscos docuit celebrare Latinos,
quo puer ipse modo, secum quo Troïa pubes;
sentences.l:
This custom of riding and these contests first
Ascanius, when with walls Long Alba he girded,
brought back, and the ancient taught to celebrate, the Latins,
in the way he himself as a boy, in the way with him the Trojan youth;
sentences.i: This manner of riding and these contests Ascanius first brought back with him, when he was circling Alba Longa with walls, and taught the Latins of old to keep them, in the same way he had kept them himself as a boy, and the Trojan youth with him;
sentences.n: 'Hunc morem cursus atque haec certamina' are the objects of 'rettulit' and 'docuit… celebrare'; 'cursus' is a genitive (fourth declension), 'of riding'. 'Primus' is predicative, 'first', 'he was the first who…'. 'Longam… Albam' is Alba Longa, the city Ascanius was to found in Latium (Jupiter foretells it at I.271), split by 'muris cum cingeret'; 'cum cingeret' is a 'cum' clause with the imperfect subjunctive, 'when he was girding'. 'Rettulit' is 'brought back', 'revived', a Trojan custom renewed in Italy. 'Priscos… Latinos' is 'the ancient Latins', the people of Latium then. 'Quo… modo… quo' is 'in the way in which… in which': 'quo puer ipse modo' is 'in the way he himself (did it) as a boy', with the verb left out, and 'secum quo Troïa pubes' 'the way the Trojan youth (did it) with him'. 'Troïa' is the adjective 'Troius', 'Trojan', in the feminine with 'pubes'; the two dots show that 'o' and 'i' are separate syllables, as against 'Troia', the city (the Latin Library prints 'Troia', the same word without the mark).

sentences.t: Albani docuere suos;
sentences.l: The Albans taught their own;
sentences.i: The Albans taught their own sons;
sentences.n: 'Docuere' is 'docuerunt'. 'Suos' is 'their own (people)', their sons: the custom passes down at Alba.

sentences.t:
hinc maxima porro
accepit Roma, et patrium servavit honorem;
sentences.l:
from there, greatest, further on
received it Rome, and the ancestral kept the honour;
sentences.i: from them in turn mighty Rome received it, and has kept up this observance of her fathers;
sentences.n: 'Hinc' is 'from here', 'from them'; 'porro' is 'further on', 'in turn', of the handing on in time. 'Maxima… Roma' is 'greatest Rome', split by 'porro accepit', with 'Roma' the subject. 'Patrium… honorem' is 'the ancestral honour', the rite of their fathers, and 'servavit' is 'has preserved'. Augustus revived the Troy game at Rome, and Virgil's readers had seen it ridden.

sentences.t: Troiaque nunc pueri, Troianum dicitur agmen.
sentences.l: and 'Troy' now it is called, the boys 'the Trojan column'.
sentences.i: and now the game is called 'Troy', and the boys 'the Trojan troop'.
sentences.n: 'Troia' is the name of the game itself, the 'Troy ride' ('lusus Troiae'), the subject of 'dicitur' with the custom (596) understood; 'pueri… Troianum dicitur agmen' is 'the boys are called the Trojan column', the one 'dicitur' doing duty for both clauses: in the second it stays singular, agreeing with the predicate 'agmen' rather than with 'pueri'. 'Nunc' is 'now', in Virgil's own day.

sentences.t: Hac celebrata tenus sancto certamina patri.
sentences.l: Thus far were celebrated, for the holy father, the contests.
sentences.i: Thus far the games were held in honour of the hallowed father.
sentences.n: 'Hac… tenus' is 'hactenus', 'thus far', split in two by 'celebrata' (tmesis, the cutting of a compound word). 'Celebrata' is a perfect participle passive with 'sunt' left out, agreeing with 'certamina'. 'Sancto… patri' is a dative, 'for the holy father', Anchises, now honoured as something like a divinity at his tomb.

sentences.t: Hic primum fortuna fidem mutata novavit.
sentences.l: Here first fortune, changed, her faith renewed.
sentences.i: Here for the first time fortune changed, and broke faith with them anew.
sentences.n: A new paragraph: the turn of the story. 'Hic' is 'here', 'at this point' (the Latin Library prints 'Hinc', 'from this point', with much the same sense). 'Fortuna… mutata' is 'fortune, changed'. 'Fidem… novavit' is literally 'renewed her faith', that is, 'made her loyalty new', changed it: after the good luck of the games, fortune is faithless once more.

sentences.t:
Dum variis tumulo referunt sollemnia ludis,
Irim de caelo misit Saturnia Iuno
Iliacam ad classem, ventosque adspirat eunti,
multa movens, necdum antiquum saturata dolorem.
sentences.l:
While with varied at the mound they pay the solemn rites, games,
Iris from the sky sent Saturnian Juno
to the Ilian fleet, and winds she breathes on her going,
many things stirring, not yet sated as to her ancient pain.
sentences.i: While they were paying their solemn rites at the tomb with games of every kind, Saturnian Juno sent Iris down from heaven to the Trojan fleet, breathing favouring winds on her way, plotting many things, and not yet having had her fill of her old resentment.
sentences.n: 'Dum… referunt' is 'while they are paying', 'dum' with the present indicative. 'Variis… ludis' is an ablative of means, 'with various games', framing the line; 'tumulo' is a dative or ablative of place, 'at the mound', Anchises's tomb, and 'sollemnia' is a neuter plural, 'the solemn rites', the anniversary offerings. 'Irim' is the Greek accusative of 'Iris', the messenger goddess whose path is the rainbow. 'Saturnia Iuno' is Juno, daughter of Saturn, the title Virgil gives her when she is hostile (as in Book I). 'Iliacam ad classem' is 'to the Ilian (Trojan) fleet', the preposition set between adjective and noun. 'Adspirat' is Greenough's spelling of 'aspirat', 'breathes (winds) on', with 'eunti' a dative participle, 'on her as she goes'. 'Multa movens' is 'stirring many things', 'scheming much'. 'Necdum… saturata dolorem' is 'not yet sated as to her grief': 'saturata' is the perfect participle passive of 'saturo', with 'dolorem' an accusative of respect (the Greek construction), and 'antiquum' recalls the 'old' grievances of Book I, the judgment of Paris and the rest.

sentences.t:
Illa, viam celerans per mille coloribus arcum,
nulli visa cito decurrit tramite virgo.
sentences.l:
She, her way hastening along a bow of a thousand colours,
seen by none, by a swift path ran down, the maiden.
sentences.i: Speeding her way along her bow of a thousand colours, the maiden ran down by a swift path, seen by no one.
sentences.n: 'Illa' is Iris, and 'virgo', 'the maiden', closes the unit on her. 'Viam celerans' is 'hastening her way', 'celerans' a present participle of 'celero'. 'Per mille coloribus arcum' is 'along the bow of a thousand colours', the rainbow: 'mille coloribus' is an ablative of quality set inside 'per… arcum'. 'Nulli visa' is 'seen by no one', 'nulli' a dative of the agent with the perfect participle. 'Cito… tramite' is 'by a swift path', an ablative of the way by which.

sentences.t:
Conspicit ingentem concursum, et litora lustrat,
desertosque videt portus classemque relictam.
sentences.l:
She spies the huge gathering, and the shores surveys,
and the deserted harbours sees and the fleet left behind.
sentences.i: She looks on the vast throng, and scans the shores, and sees the harbour empty and the fleet abandoned.
sentences.n: 'Conspicit', 'lustrat', 'videt' are vivid presents. 'Ingentem concursum' is 'the huge crowding together', the crowd at the games. 'Lustrat' is 'surveys', 'passes her eyes over'. 'Desertos… portus' is 'the deserted harbours', a plural for the one harbour, and 'classem… relictam' is 'the fleet left behind', 'relictam' the perfect participle passive of 'relinquo': the men are all at the games.

sentences.t:
At procul in sola secretae Troades acta
amissum Anchisen flebant, cunctaeque profundum
pontum adspectabant flentes.
sentences.l:
But far off on the lonely, set apart, the Trojan women, shore,
lost Anchises were weeping, and all the deep
sea were gazing at, weeping.
sentences.i: But far off, apart on a lonely beach, the Trojan women were weeping for Anchises whom they had lost, and as they wept they all gazed out at the deep sea.
sentences.n: 'At' turns from the empty fleet to the women. 'In sola… acta' is 'on the lonely shore', 'acta' a Greek word for 'beach', framing 'secretae Troades', 'the Trojan women, apart' ('Troades' is a Greek nominative plural, 'Trojan women'). 'Amissum Anchisen' is 'Anchises lost', 'Anchisen' a Greek accusative. 'Flebant' and 'adspectabant' (Greenough's spelling of 'aspectabant') are imperfects, 'were weeping', 'kept gazing at'. 'Profundum pontum' is 'the deep sea', split across the line. 'Flentes' repeats 'flebant': they weep as they look.

sentences.t:
“Heu tot vada fessis
et tantum superesse maris!
sentences.l:
“Alas, that so many shallows for the weary
and so much to be left of sea!”
sentences.i: “Alas, to think that so many waters, so much sea, still lie ahead of us, weary as we are!”
sentences.n: The print has 'maris! ”vox', the closing mark of the women's cry set after the space and joined to the next word, a misprint for 'maris!” vox' (as it stands it looks like a new opening). t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source; l and i close the cry after 'maris!'. 'Heu… superesse' is an exclamatory accusative and infinitive (you saw it with 'Mene… desistere' in Book I): 'alas, that so many shallows remain!' 'Tot vada… et tantum… maris' is the subject of 'superesse', 'vada' (properly 'shoals', 'shallows') standing for the waters of the sea, and 'maris' a partitive genitive with 'tantum', 'so much of sea'. 'Fessis' is a dative, 'for (us) weary ones'.

sentences.t: ”vox omnibus una.
sentences.l: One voice for all.
sentences.i: So they all cried with a single voice.
sentences.n: The mark ” before 'vox' is the misprinted closing mark of the women's cry (see the note on the previous unit). 'Vox omnibus una' is 'one voice to all', with 'erat' left out: 'omnibus' is a dative of possession (you've seen it with 'sunt mihi').

sentences.t: Urbem orant; taedet pelagi perferre laborem.
sentences.l: A city they beg; it wearies them of the sea to endure the toil.
sentences.i: They pray for a city; they are sick of enduring the hardship of the sea.
sentences.n: 'Urbem orant' is 'they beg for a city', 'oro' with the accusative of the thing asked for. 'Taedet' is impersonal, 'it wearies', with the persons (them) understood in the accusative and the infinitive 'perferre' as subject: 'it wearies them to endure to the end'. 'Pelagi… laborem' is 'the toil of the sea', 'pelagus' a Greek neuter noun.

sentences.t:
Ergo inter medias sese haud ignara nocendi
conicit, et faciemque deae vestemque reponit;
sentences.l:
Therefore into their midst herself, not unknowing of harming,
she throws, and both the face of a goddess and the dress she lays aside;
sentences.i: So she, no stranger to the art of doing harm, flings herself into their midst, and puts off a goddess's face and dress;
sentences.n: 'Ergo' is 'therefore', 'and so'. 'Inter medias' is 'into the midst of (them)', the women. 'Sese… conicit' is 'throws herself', 'sese' an emphatic form of 'se'. 'Haud ignara nocendi' is 'not ignorant of harming', an understatement for 'well practised in harm': 'nocendi' is a gerund in the genitive after the adjective. 'Faciemque deae vestemque' is the double '-que… -que', 'both the face and the dress of a goddess'. 'Reponit' is 'lays aside', 'puts away'.

sentences.t:
fit Beroë, Tmarii coniunx longaeva Dorycli,
cui genus et quondam nomen natique fuissent;
sentences.l:
she becomes Beroë, of Tmarian the wife, aged, Doryclus,
to whom family and once a name and sons had been;
sentences.i: she becomes Beroë, the aged wife of Doryclus of Tmarus, a woman who had once had birth and name and sons;
sentences.n: 'Fit' is 'becomes', 'turns into'. 'Beroë' is a Greek name, the two dots marking 'o' and 'e' as separate syllables (the Latin Library prints 'Beroe'). 'Tmarii… Dorycli' is 'of Tmarian Doryclus', 'Tmarius' meaning from Tmarus, a mountain in Epirus in north-western Greece; the two words enclose 'coniunx longaeva'. 'Coniunx longaeva' is 'long-lived wife', 'aged wife'. 'Cui… fuissent' is a relative clause with the pluperfect subjunctive, giving the reason she was a good choice: 'since she had once had…'; 'cui' is a dative of possession. 'Genus et… nomen natique' is 'birth, name and sons', a woman of standing, whose word would carry weight.

sentences.t: ac sic Dardanidum mediam se matribus infert:
sentences.l: and thus of the Dardanids into the midst herself to the mothers she brings:
sentences.i: and in this guise she makes her way into the midst of the Trojan mothers:
sentences.n: 'Ac sic' is 'and so', 'in this shape'. 'Dardanidum' is a genitive plural in '-um' (the first-declension Greek form, for '-arum'), 'of the Dardanids', the descendants of Dardanus, here with 'matribus', 'the Trojan mothers'. 'Mediam se… infert' is 'brings herself into the middle', 'mediam' agreeing with 'se'; 'matribus' is a dative with the compound 'infert', 'among the mothers'. The colon leads to her speech.

sentences.t:
“O miserae, quas non manus inquit Achaïca bello
traxerit ad letum patriae sub moenibus!
sentences.l:
“O wretched women, whom not the hand,” she says, “Achaean in war
dragged to death under the walls of the fatherland!
sentences.i: “Unhappy women,” she says, “whom no Greek hand dragged off to death in the war beneath the walls of our native city!
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and the start of the disguised Iris's speech, which runs to 640. 'Inquit' stands in the middle of the speech: a parenthesis, 'she says'; the print gives it no commas, and t keeps the print (l and i set it off, as the sense requires). 'O miserae' is a vocative, 'O wretched women'. 'Quas non… traxerit' is a relative clause with the perfect subjunctive, giving the reason they are wretched: 'you whom no Achaean hand dragged'. 'Manus… Achaïca' is 'the Achaean (Greek) hand', the two dots marking 'a' and 'i' as separate syllables. 'Ad letum' is 'to death'. 'Patriae sub moenibus' is 'beneath the walls of the fatherland', Troy. Better, she says, to have died there.

sentences.t:
O gens
infelix, cui te exitio Fortuna reservat?
sentences.l:
O race
unhappy, for what destruction does Fortune keep you?
sentences.i: Unhappy race, for what ruin is Fortune saving you?
sentences.n: 'O gens infelix' is a vocative, split across the line. 'Cui… exitio' is a dative of purpose, 'for what destruction', and 'te' is the race addressed. 'Reservat' is 'keeps back', 'reserves'. 'Fortuna' is personified, with the capital as Greenough prints it.

sentences.t:
Septuma post Troiae exscidium iam vertitur aestas,
cum freta, cum terras omnes, tot inhospita saxa
sideraque emensae ferimur, dum per mare magnum
Italiam sequimur fugientem, et volvimur undis.
sentences.l:
The seventh after Troy's destruction now is turning, the summer,
while straits, while lands all, so many inhospitable rocks
and stars having measured out, we are carried, while over the sea great
Italy we pursue, fleeing, and are rolled by the waves.
sentences.i: The seventh summer since the fall of Troy is now passing, while we are carried over every strait and every land, across so many cruel rocks and under so many stars, always chasing through the great sea an Italy that flees before us, tossed by the waves.
sentences.n: 'Septuma' is Greenough's spelling of 'septima', 'seventh' (as in 'maxumus'), agreeing with 'aestas', and 'exscidium' is his spelling of 'excidium', 'destruction'. 'Vertitur' is 'is turning', 'is rolling round'. Dido said 'septima aestas' to Aeneas at I.755, a year before this; the inconsistency is Virgil's. 'Cum… ferimur' is a temporal 'cum' with the indicative, 'during which time we are borne'. 'Freta… terras… saxa sideraque' are objects of 'emensae', the perfect participle of the deponent 'emetior', 'having measured out', 'having traversed', in the feminine because the women are speaking: they have travelled under the stars as well as over sea and land. 'Inhospita' is 'unwelcoming'. 'Dum… sequimur' is 'while we pursue', and 'Italiam… fugientem' is 'Italy fleeing', always receding before them. 'Volvimur undis' is 'we are rolled by the waves', 'undis' an ablative of means.

sentences.t:
Hic Erycis fines fraterni, atque hospes Acestes:
quis prohibet muros iacere et dare civibus urbem?
sentences.l:
Here are the bounds of Eryx, brotherly, and our host Acestes:
who prevents walls to lay and to give the citizens a city?
sentences.i: Here are the lands of Eryx, Aeneas's brother, and Acestes is our host: who forbids us to lay down walls and give our people a city?
sentences.n: 'Hic' is 'here', with 'sunt' left out. 'Erycis fines fraterni' is 'the brotherly territory of Eryx': Eryx, the founder-hero of the place, was a son of Venus and so half-brother to Aeneas, and 'fraterni' gives that relation to his lands. 'Hospes Acestes' is 'our host Acestes', the Sicilian king. 'Quis prohibet' is 'who prevents', with the infinitives 'iacere' and 'dare'. 'Muros iacere' is 'to lay walls', 'iacere' from 'iacio', 'throw', 'lay (foundations)', not from 'iaceo', 'lie'. 'Civibus' is a dative, 'to the citizens'.

sentences.t:
O patria et rapti nequiquam ex hoste Penates,
nullane iam Troiae dicentur moenia?
sentences.l:
O fatherland, and snatched in vain from the enemy, Penates,
will no now of Troy be called walls?
sentences.i: O homeland, O household gods rescued from the enemy in vain, shall no walls now ever be called the walls of Troy?
sentences.n: 'O patria' is a vocative, and so is 'Penates', the household gods of Troy that Aeneas carried from the burning city in Book II; 'rapti… ex hoste' is 'snatched from the enemy', and 'nequiquam' 'in vain', if they are never to have a home. 'Nullane… moenia' is 'no walls?', 'nulla' with the question enclitic '-ne', agreeing with 'moenia'. 'Troiae' is a genitive, 'of Troy', and 'dicentur' a future passive, 'will be called'.

sentences.t:
Nusquam
Hectoreos amnes, Xanthum et Simoenta, videbo?
sentences.l:
Nowhere
Hector's rivers, the Xanthus and the Simois, shall I see?
sentences.i: Shall I nowhere see rivers like Hector's, a Xanthus and a Simois?
sentences.n: 'Nusquam' is 'nowhere', set at the line-end for emphasis. 'Hectoreos amnes' is 'Hectorean rivers', the rivers of Hector's Troy. 'Xanthum et Simoenta' are the two rivers of the Trojan plain; 'Simoenta' is a Greek accusative of 'Simois'. She means rivers renamed after the old ones, as Helenus had done at Buthrotum in Book III.

sentences.t: Quin agite et mecum infaustas exurite puppes.
sentences.l: Come then, and with me the ill-omened burn up, the sterns.
sentences.i: Come, then, help me burn these ill-starred ships.
sentences.n: 'Quin' with an imperative is 'come now', 'why not': 'quin agite' is 'come on, then'. 'Agite' is the plural imperative of 'ago', used as an interjection. 'Exurite' is the plural imperative of 'exuro', 'burn up', 'burn out'. 'Infaustas… puppes' is 'the unlucky sterns', 'puppes' (the stern) standing for the whole ship, a part for the whole.

sentences.t:
Nam mihi Cassandrae per somnum vatis imago
“ardentes dare visa faces:
sentences.l:
For to me of Cassandra in sleep, the seer's, the image
burning seemed to give torches:
sentences.i: For in my sleep the phantom of the prophetess Cassandra seemed to put blazing torches in my hands:
sentences.n: The print has '“ardentes', an opening mark before 'ardentes', and another before 'hic' in 638, a misprint: the words in the line are still Beroë's narrative, and what Cassandra says in the dream is 'Hic quaerite Troiam; hic domus est… vobis' (637–638). t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source; l and i mark Cassandra's words with single marks inside the speech. 'Nam' is 'for', giving the reason. 'Mihi' is a dative, 'to me'. 'Cassandrae… vatis imago' is 'the image of Cassandra the seer', split across the line, 'vatis' in apposition: Cassandra, Priam's daughter, the prophetess whom no one believed. 'Per somnum' is 'in sleep'. 'Visa' is 'visa est', 'seemed', with the infinitive 'dare', 'to give'. 'Ardentes… faces' is 'burning torches', split by the verbs.

sentences.t:
Hic quaerite Troiam;
“hic domus est inquit vobis.
sentences.l:
‘Here seek Troy;
here is a home,’ she says, ‘for you.’
sentences.i: ‘Here seek your Troy; here,’ she said, ‘is your home.’
sentences.n: The print has '“hic domus est inquit vobis', an opening mark before 'hic' and no commas round 'inquit', a misprint for 'hic domus est,’ inquit, ‘vobis' (see the note on the previous unit); t keeps the print. Cassandra's words are here given in single marks within Beroë's speech. 'Hic' is 'here', repeated. 'Quaerite' is the plural imperative of 'quaero', 'seek'. 'Hic domus est… vobis' is 'here is a home for you', 'vobis' a dative of possession, 'you have a home here'. 'Inquit' interrupts the dream-words, 'she says', of Cassandra.

sentences.t:
Iam tempus agi res,
nec tantis mora prodigiis.
sentences.l:
Now it is time for things to be done,
and no delay with such portents.
sentences.i: Now is the time for action; there can be no delay with portents so great.
sentences.n: 'Iam tempus (est) agi res' is 'now it is time for things to be done', 'agi' the present passive infinitive of 'ago', with 'res' its subject: an idiom, 'it is time to act'. 'Nec tantis mora prodigiis' is 'and (there must be) no delay for such great portents', 'tantis… prodigiis' a dative: such signs do not allow delay.

sentences.t:
En quattuor arae
Neptuno; deus ipse faces animumque ministrat.”
sentences.l:
Look, four altars
to Neptune; the god himself torches and courage supplies.”
sentences.i: See, there stand four altars to Neptune; the god himself supplies the torches and the will.”
sentences.n: 'En' is 'look', 'see'. 'Quattuor arae Neptuno' is 'four altars to Neptune', with 'sunt' left out: altars standing on the shore, with fire on them, ready to hand. 'Deus ipse' is 'the god himself', Neptune, as though by giving fire he gives consent. 'Faces animumque' is 'torches and spirit', 'the means and the courage'. 'Ministrat' is 'supplies', the word of I.150, 'furor arma ministrat', 'fury supplies the weapons'. The closing mark ends Beroë's speech.

sentences.t:
Haec memorans, prima infensum vi corripit ignem,
sublataque procul dextra conixa coruscat,
et iacit:
sentences.l:
These things saying, first, hostile, with force she seizes the fire,
and, raised far her right hand, straining, she brandishes it,
and throws:
sentences.i: With these words she was the first to snatch the deadly fire forcibly, and lifting her right hand high, with all her strength she whirled it and threw:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Haec memorans' is 'saying these things', 'memoro' 'tell', 'speak of'. 'Prima' is predicative, 'she first', 'she was the first to'. 'Infensum… ignem' is 'the hostile fire', the fire that will harm the ships; 'vi' is the ablative of 'vis', 'with force'. 'Corripit' is 'snatches up'. 'Sublata… procul dextra' is an ablative absolute, 'her right hand raised high' ('procul', usually 'far off', here 'aloft'); 'sublata' is the perfect participle passive of 'tollo'. 'Conixa' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'conitor', 'straining', 'with an effort'. 'Coruscat' is 'brandishes', 'makes it flash'. The colon leads to the women's reaction.

sentences.t:
arrectae mentes stupefactaque corda
Iliadum.
sentences.l:
roused were the minds and amazed the hearts
of the Ilian women.
sentences.i: the minds of the Trojan women were startled, and their hearts were stunned.
sentences.n: 'Arrectae mentes stupefactaque corda' supplies 'sunt': 'minds roused, hearts stunned'. 'Arrectae' is the perfect participle passive of 'arrigo', 'set upright', 'roused', as of ears pricked up. 'Stupefacta' is from 'stupefacio', 'stun'. 'Iliadum' is the genitive plural of 'Ilias, Iliadis', 'a Trojan woman', the ordinary third-declension ending (not the old '-um' for '-orum'), and belongs to both 'mentes' and 'corda'.

sentences.t:
Hic una e multis, quae maxima natu,
Pyrgo, tot Priami natorum regia nutrix:
sentences.l:
Here one out of many, who was greatest in birth,
Pyrgo, of so many of Priam's sons the royal nurse:
sentences.i: Then one among them, the eldest of all, Pyrgo, the royal nurse of so many of Priam's sons:
sentences.n: 'Hic' is 'here', 'at this point'. 'Una e multis' is 'one from many'. 'Quae maxima natu' is 'who was greatest by birth', that is, the eldest: 'natu' is an ablative of respect, the only common form of this noun, and 'erat' is left out. 'Pyrgo' is a Greek nominative in '-o'. 'Tot Priami natorum regia nutrix' is 'royal nurse of so many of Priam's sons', the king had fifty. The verb of speaking is left out before the colon (you've seen this with 'Aeolus haec contra').

sentences.t:
“Non Beroë vobis, non haec Rhoeteïa, matres,
est Dorycli coniunx;
sentences.l:
“Not Beroë to you, not this Rhoetean woman, mothers,
is Doryclus' wife;
sentences.i: “This is not Beroë, mothers, I tell you, not the Rhoetean wife of Doryclus;
sentences.n: The opening mark begins Pyrgo's speech, which runs to 652. 'Non… non' is anaphora. 'Vobis' is an ethic dative, 'for you', 'mark you'. 'Haec' is 'this woman', the one before them. 'Rhoeteïa' is 'Rhoetean', from Rhoeteum, a headland near Troy, so 'Trojan' (the two dots mark 'e' and 'i' as separate syllables); it agrees with 'coniunx'. 'Matres' is a vocative. 'Est Dorycli coniunx' is 'is Doryclus's wife', with 'Beroë' and 'Rhoeteïa' sharing the verb.

sentences.t:
divini signa decoris
ardentesque notate oculos; qui spiritus illi,
qui voltus, vocisque sonus, vel gressus eunti.
sentences.l:
of divine beauty the signs
and burning mark her eyes; what breath to her,
what face, and of voice the sound, or the step as she goes.
sentences.i: look at the marks of divine beauty, and her blazing eyes; see what breath is in her, what a countenance, the sound of her voice, the way she walks.
sentences.n: 'Divini signa decoris' is 'the signs of divine grace', 'decus' 'beauty', 'splendour'. 'Notate' is the plural imperative of 'noto', 'mark', 'note', with the objects 'signa' and 'ardentes… oculos'. 'Qui spiritus illi' is 'what breath she has', an exclamation with 'est' left out, 'illi' a dative of possession; the questions or exclamations run 'qui… qui… vocisque… vel', and 'voltus' is Greenough's spelling of 'vultus', 'face'. 'Gressus eunti' is 'the step to her going', 'eunti' a dative present participle of 'eo', 'as she walks'. Gods were known by their gait: Venus is revealed by hers at I.405.

sentences.t:
Ipsa egomet dudum Beroen digressa reliqui
aegram, indignantem, tali quod sola careret
munere, nec meritos Anchisae inferet honores.”
sentences.l:
Myself I lately, Beroë, departing, left
sick, resentful that alone she lacked such
a rite, and would not bring the deserved to Anchises honours.”
sentences.i: I left Beroë myself a little while ago, sick, and resentful that she alone was missing such an office, and could not pay Anchises the honours he deserves.”
sentences.n: 'Ipsa egomet' is 'I myself', 'egomet' an emphatic form of 'ego'. 'Dudum' is 'a little while ago'. 'Beroen' is a Greek accusative. 'Digressa' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'digredior', 'having parted (from her)'. 'Aegram, indignantem' is 'sick, resentful', two adjectives in sequence with no 'and'. 'Quod sola careret' is 'because she alone was without', 'careo' with the ablative 'tali… munere', 'such a duty', 'such a rite'; the subjunctive gives the reason as Beroë's own thought. The print has 'inferet', a misprint for 'inferret', corrected here: the metre needs a long second syllable, which the future 'inferet' lacks, and the sense needs the imperfect subjunctive, parallel with 'careret', 'and could not bring'; t keeps the print. 'Meritos… honores' is 'the deserved honours', the funeral offerings, framed around 'Anchisae inferet'. The closing mark ends Pyrgo's speech.

sentences.t: Haec effata.
sentences.l: These things she spoke out.
sentences.i: So she spoke.
sentences.n: A half-line: Virgil left some lines unfinished (this is one of the 'hemistichs', about 58 in the poem), and Greenough prints it short. 'Haec effata' is 'effata est', 'she said these things', the perfect of the deponent 'effor', with 'est' left out.

sentences.t:
At matres primo ancipites oculisque malignis
ambiguae spectare rates miserum inter amorem
praesentis terrae fatisque vocantia regna,
cum dea se paribus per caelum sustulit alis,
ingentemque fuga secuit sub nubibus arcum.
sentences.l:
But the mothers at first doubtful, and with grudging eyes
wavering, to look at the ships, between wretched love
of the present land and, by the fates calling, the kingdoms,
when the goddess raised herself on balanced wings through the sky,
and a huge in flight cut beneath the clouds bow.
sentences.i: But the mothers at first were in two minds, and gazed at the ships with jealous eyes, torn between unhappy love for the land beneath their feet and the kingdom that called them by the will of fate, when the goddess rose into the sky on level wings, and in her flight cut a huge bow beneath the clouds.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Spectare' is a historic infinitive, used in place of the imperfect 'spectabant', 'they looked': you'll meet it again in vivid narrative. 'Ancipites' and 'ambiguae' are 'of two minds', 'doubtful', both agreeing with 'matres'. 'Oculis… malignis' is an ablative of manner, 'with grudging eyes', unfriendly to the ships that keep them at sea. 'Miserum inter amorem… regna' is 'between wretched love… and the realms', 'inter' set inside its phrase. 'Praesentis terrae' is an objective genitive, 'love of the land at hand'. 'Fatis… vocantia regna' is 'the kingdoms calling by the fates', Italy, 'fatis' an ablative of means. 'Cum… sustulit' is 'cum' with the perfect indicative after a main clause, the 'when suddenly' construction ('cum inversum'). 'Se… sustulit' is 'raised herself', from 'tollo'. 'Paribus… alis' is 'on even wings'. 'Ingentem… arcum' is the rainbow, Iris's path, framing the line, and 'fuga' 'in her flight', an ablative of manner.

sentences.t:
Tum vero attonitae monstris actaeque furore
conclamant, rapiuntque focis penetralibus ignem;
sentences.l:
Then indeed, astonished by the portents, and driven by madness,
they shout together, and snatch from the inner hearths fire;
sentences.i: Then truly, thunderstruck by the portent and driven on by frenzy, they raise a shout and seize fire from the hearths within their shelters;
sentences.n: 'Tum vero' is 'then indeed', marking the turn. 'Attonitae' is 'thunderstruck', from 'attono', and 'monstris' an ablative of cause, 'by the portents' (a plural for the one marvel). 'Actae' is the perfect participle passive of 'ago', 'driven', and 'furore' an ablative of means. 'Conclamant' is 'shout together'. 'Focis penetralibus' is an ablative of separation, 'from the inner hearths', 'penetralis' 'innermost', of the hearths in the shelters of their camp.

sentences.t:
pars spoliant aras, frondem ac virgulta facesque
coniciunt.
sentences.l:
a part strip the altars, leaves and brushwood and torches
hurl.
sentences.i: some strip the altars, and hurl leaves and brushwood and firebrands.
sentences.n: 'Pars' is singular, 'a part (of them)', with the plural verbs 'spoliant' and 'coniciunt', agreeing in sense. 'Spoliant aras' is 'strip the altars', of their fire and fuel: perhaps the four altars to Neptune of 639. 'Frondem ac virgulta facesque' are the objects of 'coniciunt', 'they throw (on the ships)'.

sentences.t:
Furit immissis Volcanus habenis
transtra per et remos et pictas abiete puppes.
sentences.l:
Rages, with loosened reins, Vulcan
benches through, and oars, and painted, of fir, sterns.
sentences.i: Fire runs wild with the reins let loose, through the benches and oars and the painted sterns of fir.
sentences.n: 'Volcanus' is Greenough's spelling of 'Vulcanus', Vulcan, the fire-god, standing for fire itself (metonymy). 'Furit' is 'rages'. 'Immissis… habenis' is an ablative absolute, 'the reins let go', the image of a charioteer giving his horses their heads. 'Transtra per' is 'through the benches', 'per' placed after its first noun (anastrophe); 'transtra' are the rowers' cross-benches. 'Pictas abiete puppes' is 'the sterns painted, of fir', 'abiete' an ablative of material, 'made of fir'; in 'abiete' the 'i' is taken as a consonant, so that the word scans in three syllables.

sentences.t:
Nuntius Anchisae ad tumulum cuneosque theatri
incensas perfert naves Eumelus, et ipsi
respiciunt atram in nimbo volitare favillam.
sentences.l:
As messenger to Anchises' tomb and to the wedges of the theatre
the burned ships he reports, Eumelus, and themselves
they look back, black in a cloud flying, the ash.
sentences.i: Eumelus brings the news of the burning ships to Anchises's tomb and the tiers of the theatre, and they look back and see for themselves the black ash flying in a cloud of smoke.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Nuntius' is 'as messenger', in apposition to 'Eumelus', the subject, held to the end. 'Ad tumulum cuneosque theatri' is 'to the tomb and the wedges of the theatre': 'cuneus' is a wedge-shaped block of seats in a Roman theatre, here the spectators at the games. 'Incensas perfert naves' is 'brings through (the news of) the ships set on fire', the participle carrying the news, a common Latin turn. 'Ipsi' is 'they themselves', with their own eyes. 'Respiciunt' is 'they look back', and it governs an accusative and infinitive, 'that the black ash is flying': 'atram… favillam' frames 'in nimbo volitare', 'in a cloud (of smoke)'.

sentences.t:
Primus et Ascanius, cursus ut laetus equestres
ducebat, sic acer equo turbata petivit
castra, nec exanimes possunt retinere magistri.
sentences.l:
First, and Ascanius, as, glad, the courses on horse
he was leading, so, keen, on horse the disturbed sought
camp, nor breathless can hold him back the masters.
sentences.i: And first of all Ascanius, just as he was, leading the horsemen's ride in glee, made eagerly on horseback for the troubled camp, and his breathless trainers could not hold him back.
sentences.n: 'Primus et Ascanius' is 'and Ascanius first', 'et' joining this to the previous unit. 'Ut… sic' is 'as… so': 'cursus ut laetus equestres ducebat' is 'as he was gladly leading the horse-runs', and 'sic' is 'just so', straight from there, without a pause (some take it 'as eagerly as he had led the ride'). 'Acer' is 'keen', 'fiery'. 'Equo' is an ablative of means, 'on his horse'. 'Turbata… castra' is 'the disordered camp', split across the line, the object of 'petivit', 'made for'. 'Exanimes' is 'breathless', 'out of breath', and 'magistri' are his riding masters, the men in charge of the boys' troops, such as Epytides.

sentences.t: “Quis furor iste novus?
sentences.l: “What madness is this new one of yours?
sentences.i: “What is this strange madness?
sentences.n: The opening mark begins Ascanius's speech, which runs to 673. 'Quis furor iste novus' is 'what this new madness', with 'est' left out: 'iste' is the demonstrative of the person addressed, 'this of yours'. 'Quis' stands here for 'qui', the interrogative adjective with 'furor'.

sentences.t:
Quo nunc, quo tenditis ”inquit,
“heu, miserae cives?
sentences.l:
Where now, where are you heading,” he says,
“alas, wretched women citizens?
sentences.i: Where now, where are you heading,” he cries, “ah, poor women of our city?
sentences.n: The print has 'tenditis ”inquit,', the closing mark set after the space and joined to 'inquit', a misprint for 'tenditis” inquit,' (as it stands it looks like an opening mark). t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source; l and i break the speech before 'inquit' and open it again at 'heu', where the print does have its opening mark. 'Quo nunc, quo tenditis' is 'where now, where are you making for', 'tendo' 'make one's way', with 'quo' repeated (anaphora). 'Miserae cives' is a vocative, 'wretched citizens', feminine because he speaks to the women ('civis' is common gender).

sentences.t:
Non hostem inimicaque castra
Argivum, vestras spes uritis.
sentences.l:
Not the enemy and the hostile camp
of the Argives, your hopes you are burning.
sentences.i: It is not the enemy, not a hostile camp of the Greeks you are burning, but your own hopes.
sentences.n: 'Non hostem inimicaque castra Argivum' is 'not the enemy and the hostile camp of the Argives': 'Argivum' is the old genitive plural in '-um', 'of the Argives', the Greeks. 'Vestras spes uritis' is 'you are burning your hopes', the objects contrasted with no 'but': the ships are their hopes of Italy. 'Uritis' is from 'uro', 'burn'.

sentences.t:
En, ego vester
Ascanius!
sentences.l:
Look, I, your
Ascanius!”
sentences.i: Look at me: it is I, your Ascanius!”
sentences.n: The print has 'Ascanius! ”Galeam', the closing mark of the speech set after the space and joined to the next word, a misprint for 'Ascanius!” Galeam'. t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source; l and i close the speech after 'Ascanius!'. 'En' is 'look'. 'Ego vester Ascanius' is 'I, your Ascanius', with 'sum' left out: he names himself so that they will come to their senses, recognising him.

sentences.t:
”Galeam ante pedes proiecit inanem,
qua ludo indutus belli simulacra ciebat;
sentences.l:
His helmet before his feet he threw down, empty,
in which, at the game clad, of war images he had been stirring;
sentences.i: He flung down before his feet the helmet he had taken off, the one he had worn in the game when he was calling up his mimic battles;
sentences.n: The mark ” before 'Galeam' is the misprinted closing mark of Ascanius's speech (see the note on the previous unit). 'Galeam… inanem' is 'the empty helmet', empty because he has taken it off so that his face can be seen, the two words framing the clause. 'Proiecit' is 'threw down', perfect of 'proicio'. 'Qua… indutus' is 'clad in which', 'indutus' the perfect participle passive of 'induo' with the ablative 'qua'. 'Ludo' is 'in the game', an ablative of time or circumstance. 'Belli simulacra ciebat' takes up 'pugnaeque cient simulacra' of 585: 'he was raising images of war', 'ciebat' the imperfect of 'cieo'.

sentences.t: accelerat simul Aeneas, simul agmina Teucrum.
sentences.l: hurries at once Aeneas, at once the columns of the Teucrians.
sentences.i: Aeneas hastens up, and with him the ranks of the Trojans.
sentences.n: 'Accelerat' is 'hurries'. 'Simul… simul' is 'at the same time… at the same time', 'both Aeneas and the Trojan columns'. 'Teucrum' is the old genitive plural in '-um'.

sentences.i: But the women, in their fear, scatter here and there along the shore, and steal off to the woods and to any hollow rocks they can find;
sentences.n: 'Ast' is an old, poetic form of 'at', 'but'. 'Illae' is 'they', the women. 'Diversa… per litora' is 'over the scattered shores', 'diversa' 'in different directions', and 'passim' 'here and there'. 'Metu' is an ablative of cause, 'from fear'. 'Diffugiunt' is 'scatter in flight'. 'Sicubi' is 'si alicubi', 'if anywhere', 'wherever there are': 'silvasque et sicubi concava… saxa' is 'the woods, and (any) hollow rocks, if there are any'. 'Furtim' is 'stealthily'.

sentences.t:
piget incepti lucisque, suosque
mutatae adgnoscunt, excussaque pectore Iuno est.
sentences.l:
it irks them of the deed and of the light, and their own,
changed, they recognise, and shaken out of their breast Juno is.
sentences.i: they are ashamed of what they have done and loath to face the daylight; changed, they know their own people again, and Juno is driven out of their hearts.
sentences.n: 'Piget' is impersonal, 'it irks', 'it shames', with the genitives of the thing, 'incepti' ('the undertaking', a perfect participle used as a noun) and 'lucis' ('the light'), and the persons understood: they are sorry for what they did and cannot bear the light of day. 'Suos' is 'their own (people)', their husbands and sons. 'Mutatae' is 'changed', in mind. 'Adgnoscunt' is Greenough's spelling of 'agnoscunt', 'they recognise'. 'Excussa… est' is the perfect passive of 'excutio', 'shake out', 'Iuno' its subject and 'pectore' an ablative of separation: Juno's madness, which was in them, has been shaken from their breasts, a striking way of naming the goddess for her influence.
